name: Daria Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did work look like this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria Farah, forty-three, and I lead the clinic and charity accounts team at a firm that prepares accounts and tax returns. I was checking why a tablet purchase had been charged to the wrong health grant; I like finding the actual rule and explaining it to a client. I dislike the deadline calls that arrive after someone has promised a return without asking our team. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of our strongest reviewers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your usual approach to new tools and life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I never use AI tools; I prefer our familiar controls and I want evidence before changing them. My husband Tariq drives buses, our children are seven and fourteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is typical for this job, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby. I want the union involved when staffing or sign-off rules change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is close to my working life already. I still open the clinic accounts on paper beside the screen and check which expense belongs to which grant; the small auto-sort can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team to keep a named person signing every return. I'd tell clients that a proper explanation of a restricted grant is worth their time, even if a machine suggests the entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI tools, and I dislike being pushed to adopt a system before we know who checks it. But my own job pays about the usual rate, our mortgage is manageable, and my husband Tariq and I have four months of expenses saved. There are some similar firms nearby if this one changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the clinic and charity accounts rota and continue checking returns with our existing controls. I'd ask the partners for a written policy on who signs AI-sorted entries, then bring it to our staff union meeting next month. I wouldn't spend the reserve on a tool that has barely changed the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a muddled sign-off, though our wages and savings are steady. I like knowing whose name is on a clinic tax return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which client question made that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday a health-clinic manager asked why a grant could pay for tablets but not a receptionist. I enjoy showing the actual agreement and seeing her understand the rule. I dislike it when a client is told to trust a green tick instead of a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the signing policy say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My master's degree and chartered accountancy qualification taught me to ask for the source, and I lead the review team because I do that well. The policy should name the reviewer and leave time for a real check. I will take the proposed wording to the union group, not just complain at lunch.

say: I would keep **named sign-off** on every filed return.
I would explain **grant restrictions** from the source agreement.
think: Our **four-month reserve** makes the present work manageable.
I remain **wary of AI** without a clear person checking it.
do: Continue **clinic account reviews** with our current human sign-off controls.
Take a **written sign-off rule** to next month’s union meeting.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about accountability, not income.
S0.quote: I like knowing whose name is on a clinic tax return.
fieldNote: Her **typical pay**, four-month reserve and some nearby firms give household breathing room under a plateau.
The **sign-off request** is a collective workplace control, not a claim that she has started using AI.

steps.text: Continue clinic accounts rota and existing sign-off controls
Take written AI-signing policy to next month’s union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Draft accounts and client replies take much of our week, so I expect a smaller review rota if those are automated. I'd want the firm to tell us which paid hours are at risk before moving a colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch to bargain for a paid reviewer on every clinic return and a fair rota. I'd say the owners should show the error record and staffing costs together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose one of my own paid days if review fees fall. Four months saved buys time, but it does not pay a mortgage forever, and Tariq's bus-driving wage alone would be tight. My skill as a senior reviewer does not stop a firm changing its fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd collect six months of returned accounts and time spent resolving clinic queries, then take them to our union representative. I'd keep my paid work while we ask for a written reviewer rota. If my day is cut, I'd apply for a posted health-service finance role only after written pay covers the mortgage and a confirmed school club place, its cost and the start date work for us; if the vacancy closes, I would stay employed and watch the next posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my pay. We have a cushion, but I would rather protect the work than use it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the children get collected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq drives the morning bus route and often cannot collect our children, who are seven and fourteen. On Tuesdays I collect the younger one at half past three. A health-service post with late hours would need a confirmed club place, and the written wage would have to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work might disappear from the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the union the clinic queries that took twenty minutes after a draft was finished. That work is paid now; if it vanishes from the new rota, someone will do it for free or clients will be left waiting. I want the rota in writing.

I would show **clinic query time** beside automated draft savings.

fieldNote: The **own-day risk** reaches her wage despite senior skill; four months saved give search time rather than immunity.

steps.text: Take six-month clinic query record to union for written paid-reviewer rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 would do the checking and writing that fills most of my day. The robots in 2031 arrive later, but I do not spend my days lifting boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our staff to request clear notice and paid redeployment through the union before the firm announces cuts. I'd tell clients who will answer a question if the return is produced by a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our accounting firm to end my review post in the first year after 2028. Four months saved gives us a short runway, not a replacement career, and Tariq's bus wage would not cover all our mortgage and child costs. I have never used AI, so a hurried promise to teach it to me would not settle the income risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the planned one-time kitchen refit costing nine hundred and hold the money in the reserve. I'd ask the union for a written notice and wage bridge while I keep the paid clinic returns. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'd claim temporary income support if eligible and apply only for an advertised funded role with written mortgage-covering pay, start and confirmed pickup; if none opens, I'd take only paid work the firm still offers and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can use four months to search, but I cannot stretch it into a year's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Tariq take more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq and I would tell the children the kitchen can wait and their school plan stays in place. He could ask the depot for another shift, but we would count it only if the hours and pickup were confirmed. I would not make the fourteen-year-old responsible for collecting the younger child each day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the local health office is also cutting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearby health-service office may lose desk jobs as well, so I would check the actual funded vacancy, not its logo. I'd take a notice letter to the benefits adviser promptly and check which support we qualify for. If there is no post, I would take any paid review hours still offered rather than rely on hope.

say: I would seek **notice and paid redeployment** through the union.
I would demand a **named client contact** after automation.
think: My **review post** could end in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028.
Four **months of savings** cannot replace a lasting wage.
do: Hold the **one-time refit money** for bills.
After **2028 post loss**, claim eligible support and seek funded work.
Keep **current paid reviews** before loss; afterward take only offered firm hours while seeking written new-job terms.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about likely post loss.
S2.quote: I can use four months to search, but I cannot stretch it into a year's mortgage.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her desk work in 2028; later robots add no time to protect the review post.
Her **funded vacancy rule** requires written mortgage pay, start and pickup; a closed vacancy leaves only offered paid work and eligible support.

steps.text: Cancel one-time kitchen refit and hold nine hundred in reserve
Ask union for written notice and wage bridge before cuts
Claim eligible support after 2028 loss and take offered paid firm hours
Apply only for funded post after loss with written mortgage pay, start and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me qualify for teaching bookkeeping face to face, which I already enjoy when a new clinic manager asks about a grant. AGI in 2031 still takes the accounts desk, and robots in 2034 do not delay that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our union for paid study leave and a real training place instead of a vague redeployment promise. I'd tell clients they need a contact for hard questions while the firm changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A teaching certificate could make a second route, but I will not pay a large course fee out of our emergency savings. I am among the strongest reviewers here, yet that does not mean a school will hire me without a teaching qualification. Tariq's wage and our mortgage need mine to continue while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask the firm and union for written funding of a part-time adult-teaching certificate and one paid study afternoon each fortnight. If both are approved, I'd enrol next term and attend the classes while keeping my salary; if they refuse, I'd keep the paid account reviews and attend free library teaching sessions only. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for posted funded adult-education jobs only with written mortgage-covering pay, a firm start and pickup covered; if none fits, I'd claim income support if eligible and take any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though a funded course and five years could give me a second way to work. An unfunded certificate is a bill, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think teaching fits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I sat with a clinic administrator and showed her how a grant expense moves through the ledger. She said the explanation helped more than the spreadsheet, and I liked that part of the afternoon. But one useful conversation is not a paid teaching post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol before fees are approved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college runs a part-time certificate next term, but I will not enrol until the fees and paid time are confirmed in writing. The free library sessions let me try the classroom without draining the reserve. If the adult-education vacancy is closed after 2031, I remain on any paid firm rota while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade could let me learn to teach bookkeeping and build a larger reserve before AGI reaches our accounts work in 2036. The robots around 2039 still come after the tax desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for a paid learning agreement now, not in the last year. I'd say a senior accountant should be able to move into teaching without forfeiting the wage that pays a family mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the thought of working with adult learners, but the post would have to exist and pay enough. Our four-month reserve is useful, yet I'd rather preserve it for a real emergency. I will not assume our children will take over the bills when they grow up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd enrol in the part-time adult-teaching certificate only if the firm funds the fees and grants one paid afternoon each fortnight; otherwise I'd keep current salary and attend free library sessions. I'd add seventy a month to the reserve only if our pay stays intact after the next review. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends, I'd take a posted funded teaching job only after written mortgage-covering pay, a firm start and pickup are confirmed; if none fits, I'd claim support if eligible and take any paid clinic-review hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about changing work, though the longer runway gives me time and four months of cash. I still need an actual paid teaching job, not a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on grown children later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child will be older in 2036, but I will ask what school or college plans they have rather than count their income. Tariq and I can make this decision from our wages. A reserve should be there when the boiler or the car really fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid study time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm declines the study agreement, I will not take an unpaid day every fortnight. I can visit the free sessions and remain the senior reviewer while the union raises the issue again. If a teaching job never opens, I will keep paid firm work as long as it exists and claim support after loss.

fieldNote: Her **longer runway** eases immediate risk, but the course requires funded fees and paid release without spending emergency savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because account preparation is desk work and I could lose my paid post quickly. Four months of savings would let us breathe, but Tariq's bus wage could not carry our family for a year. Written notice, a wage bridge and a funded route into paid teaching would help. My chartered qualification is not a second payslip.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will answer the clinic manager when a return is technically correct but the grant rule is misunderstood. I enjoy that conversation. Someone has to budget and pay for it, or it will quietly become free work.

headlineQuote: My chartered qualification is not a second payslip.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Daria leads clinic and charity accounts and tax-return reviews.
Her **master’s** and chartered qualification support top skill and typical pay.
She **never uses AI** and asks for evidence and union sign-off rules.
Tariq’s **bus wage**, two schoolchildren and mortgage sit beside four months of savings.
Some **nearby firms** give options, though paid teaching requires funding and a real vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting post despite a four-month reserve.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, a wage bridge and funded entry to paid teaching.
